---
title: "bonFIRE: calling peaks, haplotype-selective peaks"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
params:
  input_dir: "/path/to/output_dir/prefix/"
  prefix: "prefix"
  exclude_runs: ""
  min_fire_cov: 4
  min_frac_acc: 0.2
  diff_threshold: 0.25
  min_hap_cov: 10
  #fdr_cutoff: 0.05
  fisher_p_cutoff: 0.05
---

This vignette walks through the steps of `downstream/process_consensus_peak_output.R`, which starts
from the outputs of the bonFIRE pipeline in `<output_dir>/<prefix>/`:

- `<prefix>_final_tbl_w_metadata.tsv.gz`: one row per consensus peak per sample haplotype
- `<prefix>_consensus_peak_summary.tsv`: one row per consensus peak
- `<prefix>_transferred_cons_peaks_native_sequences_from_main_output.bed.gz`: the sequence of each
  consensus peak on each assembly

(see the README for their columns). The script performs the same steps without the explanations; for a
large run, use it as a batch job, since the table can need tens of GB of memory (about 40 GB for 78 HPRC
assemblies).

Every cutoff is a parameter. Change them in the header above, or when rendering:

```r
rmarkdown::render("docs/vignettes/vignette_process_main_output_and_consensus_peak_summary.Rmd",
                  params = list(input_dir = "/path/to/output_dir/my_run/", prefix = "my_run",
                                exclude_runs = "HG002_PS01015_PacBio", fisher_p_cutoff = 0.05))
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(data.table)
library(Biostrings)
library(ggplot2)

input_dir = sub("/*$", "/", params$input_dir)
tbl = fread(paste0(input_dir, params$prefix, "_final_tbl_w_metadata.tsv.gz"))
cons_peak_summary = fread(paste0(input_dir, params$prefix, "_consensus_peak_summary.tsv"))
dim(tbl)
```

# 1. Leaving out runs

There may be reason to leave out samples early in analysis. For example, you might plot coverage per consensus_peak_id per sample and realize some samples have low enough coverage that most of their data would be excluded from your analysis. Whether or not to toss these depends on your specific analysis. The code snippet below can be used to remove these samples and a subsequent step will remove any peaks that were only present in these samples (this is done after peak calling, below).

`sample_id` is the run (`sample_name` from the input file) followed by the assembly haplotype, e.g.
`HG00438_PS00991_ONT_HG00438_1`. To leave runs out of the analysis, list them in `exclude_runs`, comma-separated. You can list these as substrings of the haplotypes you want removed (e.g. `HG00438_PS00991_ONT` will result in both haplotypes of this sample being removed). 

```{r exclude}
exclude_runs = if(params$exclude_runs != "") strsplit(params$exclude_runs, ",")[[1]] else character()
all_ids = unique(tbl$sample_id)
excluded = all_ids[sapply(all_ids, function(x) any(sapply(exclude_runs, grepl, x = x, fixed = TRUE)))]
excluded
tbl = tbl[!(sample_id %in% excluded)]
```

# 2. Calling peaks

A consensus peak is just a genomic region where a peak may or may not exist in the sample haplotype of interest. The parameters defined above (at least `min_fire_cov` (`r params$min_fire_cov`) FIRE reads and at least `min_frac_acc` (`r params$min_frac_acc`) of its
reads are FIRE reads (`fire_cov_OV_cov`) were used to call peaks in the HPRC dataset and are a good starting point for most analyses). 


```{r call-peaks}
tbl[, is_peak := fcoalesce(fire_coverage >= params$min_fire_cov & fire_cov_OV_cov >= params$min_frac_acc, FALSE)]

## consensus peaks that are a peak in no sample haplotype are dropped
peaks_called = unique(tbl[is_peak == TRUE, consensus_peak_id])
tbl = tbl[consensus_peak_id %in% peaks_called] ## removes any consensus peak id's not called a peak in any sample. 
cons_peak_summary = cons_peak_summary[consensus_peak_id %in% peaks_called]

## peaks called in each sample haplotype
tbl[, .(consensus_peaks = .N, called_peaks = sum(is_peak)), by = sample_id]
```

For each consensus peak, three counts are added to the summary: the number of sample haplotypes
(`sample_id`) it is a peak in, the number of assembly haplotypes (`asm`) it is a peak in, and the number
of assembly haplotypes it could be transferred to. The first two differ only when an assembly has more
than one run (e.g. several tissues from one donor). Peaks on chrX, chrY, chrM and those without a
chromosome (`AMB`) are marked as not autosomal: the next section leaves them out.

```{r summary}
cons_peak_summary = merge(cons_peak_summary,
                          tbl[is_peak == TRUE, .(num_sample_haps_with_peak = uniqueN(sample_id)), by = consensus_peak_id],
                          by = "consensus_peak_id", all.x = TRUE)
cons_peak_summary = merge(cons_peak_summary,
                          tbl[is_peak == TRUE, .(num_asms_with_peak = uniqueN(asm)), by = consensus_peak_id],
                          by = "consensus_peak_id", all.x = TRUE)
cons_peak_summary = merge(cons_peak_summary,
                          tbl[!is.na(asm_chr), .(num_asms_with_genomic_location = uniqueN(asm)), by = consensus_peak_id],
                          by = "consensus_peak_id", all.x = TRUE)
cons_peak_summary[, autosomal := !(chr %in% c("chrX", "chrY", "chrM", "AMB"))]

cons_peak_summary[, .N, by = .(consensus_peak_asm = fifelse(consensus_peak_asm == "CHM13", "CHM13", "other assembly"), autosomal)]
```

# 3. Haplotype-selective peaks

Since the input into this pipeline are samples analyzed in a diploid reference space, we can use the consensus peak output to evaluate haplotype-selective peaks -- those with different accessibility within an individual. In the HPRC analysis, this was the starting point for identifying consensus peaks with variable accessibility across individuals (and ultimately genetic drivers of that variability) but we can do this analysis even for a single sample (diploid) run. This step combines chromatin actuation information for both haplotypes of an individual at a consensus peak onto a single line, and calculates a Fisher's exact p value used to determine haplotype-selective peaks. 


```{r haplotypes}
tbl = tbl[consensus_peak_id %in% cons_peak_summary[autosomal == TRUE, consensus_peak_id]]
tbl[, haplotype := sub("^.*_", "", sample_id)]
tbl[, sample := sub("_[^_]*$", "", sample_id)]

tbl_haplotype = dcast(tbl, consensus_peak_id + sample ~ haplotype,
                      value.var = c("coverage", "fire_coverage", "fire_cov_OV_cov"), sep = "_")
tbl_haplotype[, nonfire_1 := coverage_1 - fire_coverage_1]
tbl_haplotype[, nonfire_2 := coverage_2 - fire_coverage_2]
tbl_haplotype[, abs_hap_diff := abs(fire_cov_OV_cov_1 - fire_cov_OV_cov_2)]
```

Various thresholds can be used to call haplotype selectivity, and the ultimate choice is again dependent on the downstream application. 
A good starting point consistent with HPRC analysis is to require each haplotype to have a minimum coverage of `min_hap_cov` (`r params$min_hap_cov`), with an absolute actuation difference (abs_hap_diff) of `diff_threshold` (`r params$diff_threshold`), as well as a Fisher's exact (nominal) p-value <= .05. Here, the data is first subset to meet the first two requirements before running the Fisher's exact test, saving time and reducing the number of tests performed which becomes relevant if an FDR correction is applied.

Whether an FDR correction is applied, and how this is performed (e.g. across the whole dataset, within a tissue group, etc.) again depend both on the data (e.g. coverage) and downstream applications. Because this analysis was ultimately performed to identify genetic drivers of accessibility in the HPRC data, a process with downstream statistical funnels, only the nominal p-value was used to call haplotype selectivity, consistent with what is shown here. In your own analysis, you may want to determine a more stringent approach. 


```{r hap-test}
tbl_haplotype[, tested := fcoalesce(coverage_1 >= params$min_hap_cov & coverage_2 >= params$min_hap_cov &
                                      abs_hap_diff >= params$diff_threshold, FALSE)]
tbl_haplotype[, fisher_p := NA_real_]
tbl_haplotype[tested == TRUE, fisher_p := mapply(
  function(a, b, c, d) fisher.test(matrix(c(a, b, c, d), nrow = 2))$p.value,
  fire_coverage_1, nonfire_1, fire_coverage_2, nonfire_2)]

#tbl_haplotype[, fisher_fdr := NA_real_]
#tbl_haplotype[tested == TRUE, fisher_fdr := p.adjust(fisher_p, method = "BH")]

tbl_haplotype[, hap_selective := tested & fcoalesce(fisher_p <= params$fisher_p_cutoff, FALSE)]
tbl_haplotype[, .(pairs = .N, tested = sum(tested), hap_selective = sum(hap_selective))]

## haplotype-selective calls per run
tbl_haplotype[hap_selective == TRUE, .N, by = sample][order(-N)]
```

```{r hap-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
ggplot(tbl_haplotype[tested == TRUE],
       aes(x = fire_cov_OV_cov_1, y = fire_cov_OV_cov_2, colour = hap_selective)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "purple")) +
  labs(x = "fraction accessible, haplotype 1", y = "fraction accessible, haplotype 2",
       colour = "haplotype-selective", title = "tested pairs") +
  theme_bw()
```

# 4. Does the underlying sequence match between haplotypes?

A haplotype-selective peak whose sequence differs between the haplotypes may be driven by the sequence
change itself. Sequences are in their own file (it has no header), one row per consensus peak on each
assembly, and are joined to the table by the peak's coordinates on that assembly. An assembly contig
can run in either direction relative to the other haplotype's, so the two sequences match if they are
identical **or** one is the reverse complement of the other.

```{r sequences}
seqs = fread(paste0(input_dir, params$prefix, "_transferred_cons_peaks_native_sequences_from_main_output.bed.gz"),
             header = FALSE, col.names = c("asm_chr", "asm_start", "asm_end", "consensus_peak_id", "seq"))
seq_by_hap = merge(tbl[, .(consensus_peak_id, sample, haplotype, asm_chr, asm_start, asm_end)], seqs,
                   by = c("asm_chr", "asm_start", "asm_end", "consensus_peak_id"))
seq_by_hap = dcast(seq_by_hap, consensus_peak_id + sample ~ haplotype, value.var = "seq", sep = "_")
setnames(seq_by_hap, c("1", "2"), c("seq_1", "seq_2"))
seq_by_hap = seq_by_hap[!is.na(seq_1) & !is.na(seq_2)]
seq_by_hap[, seqs_match := seq_1 == seq_2 | seq_1 == as.character(reverseComplement(DNAStringSet(seq_2)))]

## seqs_match is NA where the peak doesn't have a sequence on both haplotypes
tbl_haplotype = merge(tbl_haplotype, seq_by_hap[, .(consensus_peak_id, sample, seqs_match)],
                      by = c("consensus_peak_id", "sample"), all.x = TRUE)
tbl_haplotype[, .N, by = .(hap_selective, seqs_match)][order(-hap_selective, seqs_match)]
```

To save the results (the script writes these two files):

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
fwrite(cons_peak_summary, paste0(params$prefix, "_consensus_peak_summary_processed.tsv"), sep = "\t", na = "NA", quote = FALSE)
fwrite(tbl_haplotype, paste0(params$prefix, "_hap_selectivity_info.tsv"), sep = "\t", na = "NA", quote = FALSE)
```
